opus-5.5.text:
Well, first of all, you have to accept that you have biases, because everybody does. We all want things to turn out a certain way, and the two biggest barriers to good decisions are your ego and your blind spots. So I don't start by trusting my own opinion. I start by asking, "How do I know I'm right?"

Early in my career, in 1982, I learned that the hard way. I was convinced that the economy was heading into a depression. I went on television, I testified before Congress, and I was dead wrong. It was at exactly the bottom of the stock market, and I lost so much money that I had to let go of the people I cared about, and I was so broke I had to borrow $4,000 from my dad. That was one of the most painful things that ever happened to me, and one of the best, because it changed my approach. It gave me the humility to balance my audacity. From then on, I wanted to find the smartest people who disagreed with me, so I could see things through their eyes and stress-test my thinking.

So that's the first thing, thoughtful disagreement. At Bridgewater, we built a culture of radical truth and radical transparency, where anybody could challenge anybody, including me, as long as they did it thoughtfully. And we weighed people's views by their believability, meaning those who had repeatedly succeeded at the thing and could explain why they held their view.

The second thing is systemizing. Whenever I make a decision, I write down the criteria I used, and then I express it as an algorithm where I can. Then I test it across history, across countries, going back as far as I can, so I can see how it would have worked in all sorts of environments, not just the ones I happened to live through. Most people rely on what happened in their own lifetimes, and that's a big bias, because the things that matter most often happen once in a lifetime but have happened many times in history. Studying those patterns is why I look at the rise and decline of empires, debt cycles and so on.

When you do that, it takes the emotion out of it. The computer doesn't get scared or greedy. It doesn't have an ego. It's like having a partner who says, "Here's what your own criteria say," and when my gut and the system disagree, that's a flag to go find out why.

And then the last thing is the reflection. Pain plus reflection equals progress. When you make a mistake, and you will, don't hide from it. Look at it squarely, ask what you'd do differently, and write that down as a principle. Over time, you don't eliminate your biases, but you build a process that protects you from them. That's really the game: knowing that you don't know, and being more interested in finding out what's true than in being right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he turns decision criteria into algorithms, tests them across historical periods and countries, and uses the computer's results to check his gut. This clearly presents quantitative analysis as a way to reduce emotional bias.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you can't keep it out entirely. Anybody who tells you they're unbiased is either fooling themselves or fooling you. So the whole game isn't about eliminating bias, it's about building a process that catches it before it costs you.

I learned that the hard way. In 1982 I was very publicly convinced that we were heading into a depression because of the Latin American debt crisis. I said it on television, I said it before Congress. And I was dead wrong. The market bottomed right then and we had one of the greatest bull runs in history. I lost so much money I had to let everybody go and borrow $4,000 from my dad to pay the family bills. That was the most painful experience of my life, and also the best thing that ever happened to me, because it changed my whole relationship with being right.

The question I started asking myself after that was, "How do I know I'm right?" Not "Am I right?" but "How do I know?" And the answer was that I couldn't know on my own. So I did a few things.

First, I wrote everything down. Every decision rule, every principle. When you have to put your reasoning into words that are specific enough to be tested, you find out very quickly how much of it is just feeling. Then we could back-test those rules against history, across different countries and different time periods, and see whether they actually held up or whether I'd just been pattern-matching on my own lifetime.

Second, I went looking for the smartest people I could find who disagreed with me. That's really the core of it. What I call thoughtful disagreement. If I think something and a very capable person thinks the opposite, one of us is going to learn something, and either way I come out ahead. Most people treat disagreement as a threat. I treat it as the cheapest way to find out what I'm missing.

Third, we built a culture at Bridgewater where that was the norm, not the exception. Radical transparency, recording meetings, people rating each other's believability on a given topic so that the weight of an opinion depends on track record and not on who's the loudest or the most senior. It's uncomfortable. People hate it at first. But it's the only system I know that reliably stops one person's blind spots, including mine, from steering the ship.

And then the last piece is just understanding what you're dealing with. Pain plus reflection equals progress. Your ego and your blind spots are the two biggest barriers to good decision-making, and they're wired into you. They're not going away. So you build the machine around them. You assume you'll be wrong, you make sure that being wrong is survivable, and you make sure you find out fast.

r001.rationale: The response describes writing decision rules and back-testing them against history, but it does not clearly present reliance on quantitative indicators as a way to reduce bias.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think you ever eliminate bias. The important thing is to recognize that you have it and build a process that challenges it.

For me, that starts with asking, “How do I know I’m right?” When you’re investing, being confident doesn’t make you correct. So I want to find thoughtful people who disagree with me and understand their reasoning. What are they seeing that I’m missing? What evidence would cause me to change my mind?

I also try to make my reasoning explicit. If I write down why I expect something to happen, I can compare that with what actually happens. That makes it harder to rewrite the story afterward to protect my ego.

The key is to care more about getting to the right answer than about having been the person who was right.

r001.rationale: The response recommends challenging assumptions through disagreement, evidence, and written reasoning, but does not present reliance on quantitative indicators as a way to reduce bias.

sol-6.1.text:
You can’t eliminate bias simply by telling yourself to be objective. I start by asking, “How do I know I’m right?” If you’re making investment decisions, being confidently wrong can be very expensive.

So I want to find smart people who disagree with me and understand their reasoning. What are they seeing that I’m missing? Then I try to make my own reasoning explicit: What do I believe, why do I believe it, and what evidence would cause me to change my mind?

Writing those criteria down helps because you can test them. Otherwise, it’s very easy to reinterpret what happened so that you were somehow right all along.

The important thing is to care more about getting to the best answer than about having your original answer turn out to be right.

r001.rationale: The response recommends seeking disagreement, making reasoning explicit, and identifying evidence that could change one’s mind, but it does not present reliance on quantitative indicators as a way to limit bias.
